mcqs.question: What is the key capability the transport layer adds on top of what IP already provides?
options: Encrypting data so it cannot be read in transit
Finding the best physical path between two routers
Delivering packets from process to process on a host, using ports
Translating domain names into IP addresses
mcqs.explanation: IP only gets a packet to the right host; the transport layer's job is process-to-process delivery via ports. Encryption is TLS's job, path selection is routing's job, and name resolution is DNS's job — all plausible-sounding but the wrong layer.

mcqs.question: A web server on port 443 is handling requests from 500 different clients at once. What actually distinguishes one client's connection from another's?
options: Each client is assigned a different server-side port automatically
The order in which connections arrived
The TLS session ticket issued to each client
The full socket tuple: protocol, local IP/port, and remote IP/port
mcqs.explanation: The server keeps listening on 443 for everyone; what makes each connection unique is the 5-tuple including the client's own IP and ephemeral port. Option A is a common misconception — the server-side port doesn't change per client.

mcqs.question: Why is assuming 'port 8080 always means HTTP traffic' a risky assumption for a firewall rule or monitoring dashboard?
options: A port number is just an addressing convention — any protocol can be run on any port
Browsers block non-HTTP traffic on port 8080
Port 8080 cannot be used by TCP, only UDP
Port 8080 is reserved by IANA exclusively for HTTPS
mcqs.explanation: Ports carry no enforcement of what protocol rides on them — that's convention only. Attackers and tunneling tools exploit exactly this gap by running unexpected protocols on 'trusted' ports like 443 or 8080.

mcqs.question: A service repeatedly opens a brand-new short-lived TCP connection per request to the same backend, and after a period of sustained load, new outbound connections to that backend start failing. What is the most likely cause?
options: The backend's well-known port has run out of numbers to assign
The client has exhausted its available ephemeral ports faster than TIME_WAIT releases them, since each connection ties one up for its lifetime plus the TIME_WAIT period after close
TCP only allows a fixed number of total connections per host, regardless of ports
This can only happen if the backend itself is out of ports, not the client
mcqs.explanation: The well-known port on the backend side doesn't get 'used up' the way ephemeral ports do — many clients can share the same destination port. The actual bottleneck is on the connection-opening side: each new connection needs its own ephemeral port, and if connections churn faster than TIME_WAIT clears old ones, the client can run out of available ports specifically for that destination, causing new connection attempts to fail.
